title: Accuracy, precision and validity in biology

draft.title: Accuracy, precision and validity
card: is how close a measurement is to the true value. A scale reading 50.0 g for a 50.0 g mass is accurate.
is how close repeated measurements are to each other. Results can be precise but not accurate.
is whether an investigation measures what it set out to measure. It needs a fair test, with only the factor being tested changing.
A result can be precise and still be off target. A study can have accurate tools but not be valid if it measures the wrong thing or other factors change.
draft.remember: Accurate is close to the true value. Precise is close together. Valid is measuring what you meant to.

a.q: A thermometer reads 24.1, 24.0 and 24.2 °C in water that is truly 20.0 °C. What describes these readings?
a.why: The readings are close to each other, so they are precise. They are not close to the true value of 20.0 °C, so they are not accurate.
a.clue: Compare the readings with each other, then with the true value.

b.q: Sam tests whether fertiliser makes bean plants grow taller. He gives the fertilised plants a sunny bench and the others a dark shelf. Why is his investigation not valid?
opts: Light also differs, so height may not be due to fertiliser
His height measurements are not close to the true value
His repeated measurements do not agree with each other
He used too few types of fertiliser in the investigation
b.why: Validity needs a fair test where only the tested factor changes. Light also changed, so Sam cannot tell whether fertiliser or light caused the difference. Accuracy is about closeness to the true value, which is a different idea.
b.clue: Count how many factors changed between the two groups.

b.best: Light also differs, so height may not be due to fertiliser
